name: Black supremacy
summary: Black Supremacy is the name Rev. Fitz Balintine Pettersburgh gave in his 1926 Royal Parchment Scroll of Black Supremacy, and Leonard Howell took over in The Promised Key (1935), for a Jamaican doctrine of a divinely ordained black triumph over white supremacy: a theocratic 'Church Triumphant' under King Alpha and Queen Omega (Haile Selassie), with whites cast as lepers, no marriage across the colour line, free compulsory education and the shooting of rapists and lynchers.
scope: Represents the doctrine named 'Black Supremacy' by Pettersburgh's 1926 Royal Parchment Scroll and Howell's c. 1935 Promised Key, as Dunkley and Crockford tie the term to them. The Nation of Islam under Elijah Muhammad is called black supremacist by watchdogs and news outlets, which are a gate only here; it is an organisation, and its platform is not evidence for this doctrine, so answers resting on it were nulled. Excludes Black Hebrew Israelite groups, the Nuwaubians, later Rastafari and black nationalism that does not claim racial superiority.

sources.title: The Royal Parchment Scroll of Black Supremacy
sources.author: Rev. Fitz Balintine Pettersburgh (Kingston, 1926)
sources.usedFor: The founding text of the name: its statements on race, marriage, education, church and government, and punishment of rapists and lynchers.

sources.title: The Promised Key
sources.author: Leonard P. Howell (published under the name G. G. Maragh, c. 1935)
sources.usedFor: Howell's 1935 tract that took over Pettersburgh's 'Black Supremacy': race, marriage, free compulsory education, theocracy, the shooting of rapists and lynchers.

sources.title: The Suppression of Leonard Howell in Late Colonial Jamaica, 1932-1954
sources.author: Dunkley, D. A., New West Indian Guide 87 (2013)
sources.usedFor: Ties the name 'Black Supremacy' to Pettersburgh's 1926 Scroll and Howell's Promised Key, and says Howell took the term over.

sources.title: Rastafari
sources.author: Susannah Crockford, Critical Dictionary of Apocalyptic and Millenarian Movements (2021)
sources.usedFor: Says early Rastafari was 'more strongly black supremacist', inverting the colonial order by claiming whites were inferior.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: The texts hold the white 'Church Militant' and its ways to be evil and the black 'Church Triumphant' to be above them; Crockford: the early movement 'tried to invert the colonial social order by claiming that white people were inferior to black people. The ways of white people were evil'.

death-penalty.rationale: Both texts order that 'rapers, mob lynchers and Klu-Klux Klan are to be shot down'; they name no other capital crimes.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Both texts forbid marriage across the colour line: 'BLACK MUST NOT MARRY WHITE NOR WHITE BLACK, "RACE ENMITY"' and 'Do not allow Black Supremacy to Marry any one from white supremacy'.

divinely-chosen-superior-people.rationale: Both texts present Black Supremacy as God's triumph over white supremacy: 'Black Supremacy has taken charge of white supremacy by King Alpha and Queen Omega', and the white 'Anglo-Saxon' is the 'leper'; Crockford says the early movement claimed that white people were inferior to black people.

free-public-college.rationale: The Promised Key: 'Education will be free and compulsory to all mortal beings, if you are not an enemy of black Supremacy'; the Scroll adds 'You may go to SCHOOL UNTIL YOU DIE'.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Both texts present a 'Holy Theocracy' under King Alpha and Queen Omega whose 'Supreme law' is read out of the Bible.

racial-pride.rationale: The texts define Black Supremacy as 'Our Triumph over white supremacy, Our SLAVE MASTER' and exalt the black race as the Church Triumphant.

separate-church-state.rationale: Black Supremacy is itself called 'The Church Triumphant' and 'Theocracy': church and government are one.

notes: Searched under the Wikipedia redirect names (Black supremacist, Black supremacism, Black racism and the rest): the defining sources that use the term are Dunkley and Crockford on Pettersburgh and Howell. The two primary texts settle few statements, so most answers are null; the Nation of Islam answers of the first pass were nulled as a coatrack. Themes searched: race, marriage, religion and state, education, punishment. The Holy Piby (Rogers) was read for the same themes and gave nothing that names Black Supremacy.
